# Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes

> *Vitamins and minerals are needed only in milligram or microgram amounts and supply almost no
> energy, yet a shortfall can blind a child, soften bone or leave permanent nerve damage, and an
> excess of some is toxic. The body also holds water and electrolytes in tight balance, and
> Singapore's signature problem with them is an excess: too much sodium.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Distinguish fat-soluble from water-soluble vitamins, and explain how a vitamin's structure relates to
  its storage and its risk of toxicity.
- Recognise the classic deficiency syndromes of the major vitamins and the groups at risk.
- Explain why folic acid is advised before conception, and why folate can mask vitamin B12 deficiency.
- Explain how bioavailability shapes the absorption of iron and calcium, and give food-first advice
  that improves it.
- Describe how water balance is regulated, and how sodium and potassium act in opposite directions on
  blood pressure.
- Judge when a micronutrient supplement or a salt substitute is justified, and when it may harm.
:::

## Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes at a glance {#sec-overview}

Unlike the macronutrients, **micronutrients** (the vitamins and minerals) supply almost no energy.
They enable the reactions that keep us alive, acting as **cofactors** (non-protein helpers that an
enzyme needs in order to work), antioxidants and structural components. We need them only in
milligram or microgram amounts, and a **food-first** pattern (a varied, mostly whole-food diet)
supplies most of them [@afn2021curriculum].

The vitamins fall into two classes that behave differently in the body:

| Class | Members | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Fat-soluble | A, D, E, K | Stored in fat and the liver → deficiency develops slowly, but toxicity is possible with megadoses |
| Water-soluble | B-complex, C | Largely not stored → need regular intake; excess is mostly excreted |

Vitamin B12 is one exception: it is water-soluble, but the liver holds years' worth, so B12
deficiency develops slowly instead of appearing within weeks.

The behaviour can often be seen in the structure itself. Vitamin C is studded with hydroxyl (–OH)
groups, so it dissolves in water and is washed out. Vitamins A and D are mostly hydrocarbon, so they
dissolve in fat and are stored, which is why they can build up to harmful levels if over-supplemented.
Switch between the three vitamins below to compare them.

<div data-island="molecule" data-src="/structures/micronutrients.mol.yml"></div>

::: {.callout-warning}
## Are more vitamins healthier?
Because vitamins are essential, it is easy to assume that more must be better. Fat-soluble vitamins
(notably A and D) can **accumulate to toxic levels**. Water-soluble vitamins are mostly excreted, but
very high intakes can still cause harm: B6 can damage nerves, and vitamin C can cause kidney stones.
What helps is regular intake, not megadoses. For most people, food beats pills.
:::

Minerals and trace elements each have a signature role:

- Calcium builds bone.
- Iron carries oxygen.
- Iodine is needed to make thyroid hormone.
- Zinc supports immunity and healing.
- Sodium and potassium maintain fluid balance and nerve and muscle function.

## The vitamins {#sec-micro-vitamins}

### Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K {#sec-fat-soluble}

Because the fat-soluble vitamins are stored, deficiency develops slowly, but supplements can build up
to harmful levels. Two of them, vitamins A and D, matter most in practice.

**Vitamin A** is needed for vision and for healthy skin, lining tissues and immunity. Its deficiency
is the world's leading preventable cause of childhood blindness: the earliest sign is night
blindness, which progresses through **xerophthalmia** (dryness of the eyes) to corneal damage
[@whoVitADef].

Vitamin A comes in two forms. **Preformed vitamin A** comes ready-made in liver, egg yolk and dairy.
**β-carotene**, a precursor in orange and dark-green produce (carrot, sweet potato, pumpkin, spinach,
kangkong), is converted to vitamin A by the body as needed. The two forms differ in safety. High-dose
preformed vitamin A is **teratogenic** (it can cause birth defects). Isotretinoin, an acne drug, is
itself a retinoid (a vitamin A derivative) and carries the same risk, which is why it demands strict
pregnancy prevention. β-carotene from food is safe, because its conversion
is self-limiting.

**Vitamin D** behaves more like a hormone than a vitamin: the body makes it in skin from a
cholesterol precursor using ultraviolet B (UVB) light, then activates it in the liver and kidney. Its
job is to help absorb calcium for bone. Deficiency causes **rickets** in children (bowed legs,
knock-knees) and **osteomalacia** in adults (soft, aching bones). Few foods carry vitamin D (oily
fish, egg yolk, fortified milk), so skin synthesis and fortification matter. Toxicity comes from
supplements, not sunlight: mis-dosed products can push blood calcium dangerously high.

![Oily fish such as salmon are one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D. Photo: DanaTentis, CC0.](/figures/food/grilled-salmon.jpg){#fig-salmon fig-alt="A grilled salmon fillet on a plate." width="320" .lightbox}

::: {.callout-note}
## Does a sunny climate prevent vitamin D deficiency?
Because skin makes vitamin D in sunlight, many assume that in a country as sunny as Singapore nobody
runs short. However, indoor work, sun avoidance, covering up and ageing all lower skin synthesis.
Deficiency is common in Singapore despite the climate: one healthy-adult sample found about 42% at
risk, higher in women, older adults and those who work indoors or cover up [@sgVitDeficiency].
:::

**Vitamin K** is needed for blood clotting. Its best-known deficiency is in newborns, who are born
with low stores and get little from the gut or from breast milk. A vitamin K injection at birth is
therefore routine, and it prevents rare but catastrophic bleeding [@aapVitK]. Adults get vitamin K
from leafy greens and fermented foods.

**Vitamin E** is an antioxidant in cell membranes, found in nuts, seeds and vegetable oils; dietary
deficiency is rare and is seen mostly with fat malabsorption [@odsVitE]. Neither vitamin K nor
vitamin E is a common toxicity concern, so the fat-soluble vitamins are not equally risky in excess.

### Water-soluble vitamins: the B-complex and C {#sec-water-soluble}

Because the water-soluble vitamins (except B12) are not stored, they need regular intake, and their
classic deficiency diseases are among the most recognisable syndromes in medicine. Investigating and
treating them is beyond the scope at this stage; the task is to recognise the pattern and the group at
risk. Each vitamin has a broad role, a classic deficiency and a group in whom that deficiency is most
likely:

| Vitamin | Broad role | Classic deficiency | Watch in… |
|---|---|---|---|
| B1 (thiamine) | Turning carbohydrates into energy | Beriberi; Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome (lasting memory loss) | Heavy alcohol use; polished-rice diets |
| B2 (riboflavin) | Energy metabolism | Cracked mouth corners, sore tongue | Poor diet; little dairy |
| B3 (niacin) | Energy metabolism | Pellagra ("3 Ds") | Maize-dependent diets; alcohol |
| B6 (pyridoxine) | Amino-acid metabolism | Neuropathy, dermatitis | Isoniazid therapy for tuberculosis; alcohol |
| B9 (folate) | DNA and cell division | Neural-tube defects; anaemia | Pregnancy; alcohol |
| B12 (cobalamin) | DNA and nerve myelin | Anaemia and nerve damage | Vegans; older adults; metformin |
| C (ascorbic acid) | Collagen; iron absorption | Scurvy | Very restricted diets; isolated older adults |

::: {.callout-note}
## Beriberi and pellagra: diseases of food processing
**Beriberi**, thiamine (B1) deficiency, appears where the staple is heavily refined. Milling strips
the thiamine-rich bran from rice, so the historical switch to polished white rice triggered epidemics
across Asia. Beriberi shows as heart failure and oedema ("wet") or as nerve damage ("dry"). In heavy
drinkers, thiamine deficiency causes **Wernicke's encephalopathy** (confusion, unsteadiness and
eye-movement problems), an emergency in which thiamine is given first [@statpearlsThiamine].

**Pellagra**, niacin (B3) deficiency, appears in maize-dependent diets and is remembered as the "3 Ds":
dermatitis (a rash on sun-exposed skin), diarrhoea and dementia [@statpearlsNiacin]. In both
diseases, how a population's staple food was processed affected whether the deficiency appeared.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Folate before conception
The neural tube closes about four weeks after conception, often before a woman knows she is
pregnant. Too little folate at that point risks **neural-tube defects** (birth defects of the brain
and spinal cord, such as spina bifida), so folate has to be adequate before conception. Women who
could become pregnant are therefore advised to take **folic acid** (the form of folate used in
supplements and fortification) from before conception into early pregnancy [@whoFolate].

Many countries now fortify flour with folic acid and have seen neural-tube defects fall, the same
logic of changing the food supply as salt reduction. Singapore does not mandate this fortification
[@ffiFortification], so the advice to take folic acid before conception carries more of the weight
here. Food sources live up to the name (Latin *folium*, leaf): dark leafy greens, beans and legumes.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Why B12 deficiency is dangerous to miss
Vitamin B12 has two jobs: making blood cells and maintaining the myelin sheath that insulates nerve
fibres. B12 deficiency therefore causes **anaemia** (a shortage of red blood cells or haemoglobin) and
nerve damage (numbness, pins and needles, an unsteady gait), and the nerve damage can become
**permanent** [@scdB12]. Giving folate can correct the anaemia while the nerve damage continues
unnoticed, so the two vitamins must be considered together. The groups to watch are vegans and strict
vegetarians (B12 is essentially absent from plant foods), older adults and people on long-term
metformin, a common diabetes medicine [@metforminB12]. A reliable plant-based intake needs fortified
foods or a supplement; spirulina and algae do not count, because they contain an inactive look-alike.
:::

**Vitamin C** builds collagen, the body's "glue", so its deficiency, **scurvy**, is a disease of
things falling apart: bleeding, spongy gums, easy bruising, poor wound healing and corkscrew-shaped
hairs [@dermnetScurvy]. Vitamin C also greatly increases the absorption of plant (non-haem) iron, so a
squeeze of lime or a vitamin C-rich fruit with an iron-rich meal helps (see [iron](#sec-iron) below).

![Citrus and other fruit are rich in vitamin C, which also helps the gut absorb plant iron. Photo: Scott Bauer, USDA (public domain).](/figures/food/citrus-fruits.jpg){#fig-citrus fig-alt="Sliced oranges, lemons and other citrus fruit." width="320" .lightbox}

::: {.callout-note}
## Does vitamin C prevent colds?
Many people take vitamin C to ward off colds. In the general population, routine vitamin C does not
prevent colds; it only slightly shortens how long they last [@cochraneVitC].
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: high-dose vitamin A supplements can harm a pregnancy, but a diet rich in carrots and sweet potato does not. Why the difference?
Preformed vitamin A is fat-soluble, so a high dose is stored rather than readily excreted, and can
accumulate to teratogenic levels. The β-carotene in orange produce is converted to vitamin A only as
needed, and this self-limiting conversion is what makes β-carotene from food safe.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient with anaemia, numbness and pins and needles is given folate, and her blood count improves. Why is that not reassuring?
Vitamin B12 is needed both to make blood cells and to maintain the myelin around nerves. Folate can
correct the anaemia of B12 deficiency while the nerve damage continues, and that damage can become
permanent. Anaemia with nerve symptoms calls for thinking about B12 and folate together, especially in
a vegan, an older adult or a patient on long-term metformin.
:::

## Minerals and trace elements {#sec-micro-minerals}

### Iron: why the source matters {#sec-iron}

Iron is the oxygen-carrying core of haemoglobin, so iron deficiency shows as fatigue, pallor and
breathlessness (the pattern in [the case](#sec-case) below). How much dietary iron reaches the body
depends on its **bioavailability**, the proportion of a nutrient in food that is absorbed. (For where
in the gut iron is absorbed, see the *Digestion & Absorption* chapter.) Two forms of dietary iron
differ in bioavailability:

Haem iron
: Iron bound in haem (the iron-containing part of haemoglobin, and of a similar protein in muscle), which comes from meat, fish and poultry. It is well absorbed and little
  affected by the rest of the meal.

Non-haem iron
: Iron not bound in haem, which comes from plants, eggs and fortified foods and is the only source
  for vegetarians. It is poorly and variably absorbed, and its absorption swings with what else is on
  the plate [@odsIron].

Because non-haem iron absorption depends on the rest of the meal, the foods eaten with it can increase
or reduce how much is absorbed:

| Increases non-haem iron absorption | Reduces non-haem iron absorption |
|---|---|
| Vitamin C (fruit, vegetables, a squeeze of lime) | Tea and coffee (tannins), which with a meal can cut absorption by more than half [@hurrell1999tea] |
| A little meat or fish in the same meal | **Phytates** (compounds that bind iron) in wholegrains, legumes and nuts |
| Soaking, sprouting or fermenting (idli, dosa, sourdough) | Calcium (for example, a large glass of milk with the meal) |

The food-first advice follows: pair iron-rich plant foods with a vitamin C-rich food, and drink tea or
coffee between meals, not with them. Because non-haem iron is absorbed less well, vegetarians and
vegans need roughly 1.8 times as much iron [@odsIron], and their intake deserves a closer look. Beyond fatigue,
two signs of iron deficiency are worth recognising: **koilonychia** (spoon-shaped nails) and **pica**
(craving non-foods, classically ice).

![Red meat is the richest source of well-absorbed haem iron; non-haem iron from plants needs more help to be absorbed. Photo: Hannahdownes, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/figures/food/red-meat.jpg){#fig-redmeat fig-alt="A cooked portion of red meat on a plate." width="300" .lightbox}

### Calcium and bone {#sec-calcium}

Over 99% of the body's calcium is in bone. Bone mass is built early in life and drawn on later, which
is why bone is often likened to a bank. About 90% of peak bone mass (the most bone a person ever has)
is laid down by about age 18–20, and bone mass peaks around age 30 [@nof_weaver_2016_pbm_position].
Adequate calcium, vitamin D (needed to absorb it) and weight-bearing activity in youth build the
reserve that protects against fractures decades later. Hip fractures are a growing burden in Singapore:
as the population ages, hip-fracture admissions nearly doubled between 2000 and 2017, even though
age-adjusted rates fell [@yong2019hipfracSG]. Low intake adds to the concern: in one Singapore cohort, about half of older
adults fell short of the calcium recommendation [@ye2023daha].

Calcium does not have to come from dairy. Its bioavailability, like iron's, depends on the food it
comes in. Some greens contain **oxalate**, a compound that binds calcium and reduces its absorption.
The calcium in calcium-set tofu and low-oxalate greens (kai-lan, bok choy, broccoli) is absorbed as
well as or better than the calcium in milk, and small fish eaten with their bones (ikan bilis,
sardines) add more. Spinach is the main exception: it is rich in calcium, but its oxalate binds
it, so it is poorly absorbed [@weaverVegCalcium1999].

![Kai-lan and other low-oxalate leafy greens are good non-dairy sources of calcium, folate and non-haem iron. Photo: Nthaci, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/figures/food/kai-lan.jpg){#fig-kailan fig-alt="Fresh kai-lan (Chinese broccoli) on a plate." width="300" .lightbox}

::: {.callout-note}
## Does everyone need a calcium supplement?
Calcium supplements are often taken as routine insurance for bone. For healthy adults, routine calcium
supplements, with or without vitamin D, have limited fracture-prevention benefit. Combined calcium and
vitamin D slightly raises the risk of kidney stones; trials have not shown a rise in cardiovascular
disease, but calcium's cardiovascular safety is still being studied [@uspstfCalcium2018]. Food first still applies: bone mass is
built from diet and activity, and supplements are reserved for people with a genuine shortfall or
osteoporosis (thinned, fragile bone), under guidance (see the *Bone & Joint Health* chapter).
:::

### Iodine and iodised salt {#sec-iodine}

Iodine's single job is to build thyroid hormone, which sets metabolic rate and drives foetal brain
development. Iodine deficiency causes **goitre** (a swollen thyroid) and, in pregnancy, irreversible
intellectual disability in the child; it is a leading preventable cause of brain injury worldwide
[@odsIodine].

Iodising salt has pushed iodine deficiency out of most of the world. Two trends can let it quietly
return: non-iodised "gourmet" salts (sea salt, pink Himalayan) and rising plant-based eating, which
reduces intake of the main sources (dairy, seafood and eggs). Keeping iodised salt as the kitchen
default guards against both.

In Singapore, salt iodisation is voluntary, not mandatory [@codling2017iodine], and no national
iodine-status survey has been published. The food supply therefore does not guarantee enough iodine,
and choosing iodised salt is a sensible individual safeguard.

![Iodised salt: a cheap population-wide fix for iodine deficiency; most "gourmet" salts are not iodised. Photo: Drtony999, CC BY-SA 3.0.](/figures/food/iodised-salt.jpg){#fig-iodisedsalt fig-alt="A small pile of fine iodised salt on a dark dish." width="300" .lightbox}

### Zinc, magnesium and selenium {#sec-trace-minerals}

**Zinc** supports immunity, wound healing and growth. Zinc deficiency shows as poor healing, a rash
around the mouth and on the hands, hair loss and blunted taste. The groups to watch are vegetarians
(phytates bind zinc as they bind iron), pregnant women and older adults [@odsZinc].

**Magnesium** is a cofactor for nerve and muscle function and for energy metabolism, drawn from
greens, wholegrains, nuts and legumes. Low levels are associated with heavy alcohol use, poorly
controlled diabetes and some medicines taken long term, such as certain diuretics (drugs that increase
urine output) and proton pump inhibitors (drugs that reduce stomach acid) [@odsMagnesium].

**Selenium** is needed by antioxidant enzymes and for thyroid metabolism. Selenium deficiency, which
depends on how much selenium the local soil holds, causes **Keshan disease**, a disease of heart
muscle. Selenium is also a nutrient whose excess is itself toxic, so a couple of Brazil nuts is plenty
[@odsSelenium].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does a vegetarian need roughly 1.8 times as much iron as someone who eats meat?
Meat supplies haem iron, which is well absorbed and little affected by the rest of the meal. A
vegetarian relies on non-haem iron, which is poorly and variably absorbed and is reduced by tea,
coffee, phytates and calcium in the same meal, so more must be eaten to absorb the same amount.
Pairing it with a vitamin C-rich food, and taking tea or coffee between meals, improves its
absorption.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does calcium intake in adolescence matter for a hip fracture at 80?
About 90% of peak bone mass is laid down by around age 18–20, and bone mass peaks around age 30.
Calcium, vitamin D and weight-bearing activity in youth build the reserve that later life draws on and
that protects against fractures decades later.
:::

## Water and electrolytes {#sec-micro-water}

### Water and hydration {#sec-water}

Water is a nutrient in its own right, and the body holds its balance of water and **electrolytes**
(charged minerals dissolved in body fluids, such as sodium and potassium) tightly. Thirst and
**antidiuretic hormone (ADH)**, the hormone that reduces water loss in urine, are the everyday
regulators, so intake roughly matches losses through urine, skin, breath and stool. Singapore's hot,
humid climate and exercise both raise needs [@afn2021curriculum].

There is no fixed number of glasses to drink. Urine colour is a simple self-check, with pale straw the
target, and problems lie at both ends of the range:

Dehydration
: Too little body water, shown by thirst, dark concentrated urine, dizziness and reduced urine output.

Over-hydration
: Rarer than dehydration, but real: drinking only plain water in large amounts during endurance
  exercise can cause dangerous **exercise-associated hyponatraemia** (low blood sodium).

Hydration therefore means water and electrolytes, not water alone.

### Sodium and potassium: opposite effects on blood pressure {#sec-sodium-potassium}

Sodium and potassium push blood pressure in opposite directions: too much sodium and too little
potassium both raise blood pressure and cardiovascular risk (see the *Cardiovascular Disease &
Hypertension* chapter). The WHO targets are less than 2,000 mg of sodium a day [@who2020diet] and
at least 3,510 mg of potassium a day [@who2012potassium]. Fruit and vegetables, the half-plate of My
Healthy Plate, are the natural potassium source [@hpbHealthyPlate].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a marathon runner plans to drink as much plain water as possible during the race. Why is that not the safest plan?
The body regulates water and electrolytes together, with thirst and ADH matching intake to losses.
Drinking only plain water in large amounts during endurance exercise can cause dangerous
exercise-associated hyponatraemia (low blood sodium). Hydration means water and electrolytes, and
there is no fixed volume that suits everyone.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does the WHO set a ceiling for sodium but a floor for potassium?
The two electrolytes push blood pressure in opposite directions: too much sodium and too little
potassium both raise blood pressure and cardiovascular risk. Sodium is therefore capped (less than
2,000 mg a day) and potassium has a minimum (at least 3,510 mg a day); fruit and vegetables, the
half-plate of My Healthy Plate, are its natural source.
:::

## When does a patient need a supplement? {#sec-close}

For most people eating a varied, mostly whole-food diet, a supplement is not needed. Micronutrients
come packaged in food with the cofactors, fibre and other nutrients that make them work, and
in adults without a known deficiency, vitamin and mineral pills have not been shown to prevent heart
disease or cancer, and β-carotene pills do more harm than good [@uspstf2022vitamins]. Supplements earn
their place for specific, identifiable needs:

- Folic acid before and in early pregnancy.
- B12 for vegans and many older adults.
- Vitamin D where skin synthesis is low.
- Iron for a diagnosed deficiency.

They are not daily insurance against a diet that could be improved, and more is not safer: the
fat-soluble vitamins and several minerals are harmful in excess. Food comes first; supplements are
for an identified need.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

Three micronutrient problems are sharply local: vitamin D deficiency is common despite the climate,
many older adults fall short on calcium, and, with salt iodisation voluntary, the food supply does not
guarantee enough iodine [@codling2017iodine].

The signature micronutrient problem in Singapore, however, is an excess: too much sodium. The
National Nutrition Survey 2022 found average sodium intake around 3,620 mg a day, close to double the
limit, with about 9 in 10 residents exceeding it [@mohNNS2022]. Most of that sodium does not come from
the salt shaker at the table. It is in sauces, broths and food eaten out of home [@mohNNS2022], which makes sodium a
hawker-culture issue. Some common hawker dishes approach or exceed a whole day's sodium in a single
bowl. (Per-dish figures from consumer-education sources are illustrative and vary by stall
[@shfSaltiestDishes].)

The population response is policy, not willpower alone. The Health Promotion Board's "Less Salt, More
Taste" movement and its work to make lower-sodium salt, sauces and seasonings affordable aim to change
the food supply itself [@hpb2023sodium]. The approach follows the same label-led logic as Nutri-Grade
for sugary drinks [@hpbNutriGrade], and the same idea as iodising salt: change the food supply as well
as individual habits.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Salt substitutes and the SSaSS trial
The Salt Substitute and Stroke Study (SSaSS) replaced regular salt with a 75% sodium, 25% potassium
substitute and cut the relative rate of stroke (about 14%), major cardiovascular events (about 13%) and
death (about 12%) over about 5 years. In absolute terms, that was about 4.5 fewer strokes for every
1,000 people followed for a year (29 versus 34) [@neal2021ssass]. Four caveats temper the result:

- It was **open-label** (participants knew which salt they were using) and **cluster-randomised**
  (groups, not individuals, were assigned to each salt).
- It ran in rural China in a specific high-risk population: people with a prior stroke, or older
  adults with hypertension (persistently raised blood pressure).
- A 2024 secondary analysis attributes most of the blood-pressure fall to the added potassium, not to
  the sodium reduction [@ssassPotassiumBP2024].
- Potassium-based substitutes carry a risk of hyperkalaemia (raised blood potassium), which makes them
  unsafe in kidney disease or with certain blood-pressure medications.

Salt substitutes are therefore **not blanket advice**, and SSaSS shows why any trial must be read
together with its caveats.
:::
